findings.asked: Define centre of gravity, mark it on an object, then say which object is least stable and why.
findings.wentWrong: Most gave the definition but some described the weight 'acting' confusingly; the least stable object was identified, but the explanation had to be about the height of the centre of gravity and often was not.
findings.rule: Stability = height of the centre of gravity and width of the base.

findings.wentWrong: Not well answered: few said the weight 'acts' there; 'gravity' was written where 'weight' was needed; some answered about balance or stability instead.
findings.rule: The point at which all the weight of the object appears to act.

findings.asked: Choose the most stable position of a beam and give the reason; mark its centre of gravity.
findings.wentWrong: The position and the centre of gravity were found, but the reason was commonly 'more area' or 'surface area' rather than a lower centre of gravity or wider base.
findings.rule: Never 'area': say lower centre of gravity or wider base.

findings.asked: Mark the centre of gravity of a ring.
findings.wentWrong: A significant number could not place it, because it lies in the empty space at the centre.
findings.rule: The centre of gravity can be outside the material of the object.

ruleToRemember: The centre of gravity is the point where all the weight of an object appears to act (say weight, not gravity); for a uniform object it is at the geometric centre, even if that is empty space. An object is more stable with a low centre of gravity and a wide base, and topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside the base.
aStarSignal: Explaining toppling with the line of action of the weight and the edge of the base, not with 'area'.
